newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH AUG MONEY SUPPLY MODEST, BUT CREDIT JUMPS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH AUG MONEY SUPPLY MODEST, BUT CREDIT JUMPS.

text.p: Poland's modest rise in broad money in August bode well for stifling price growth in that month, but a quick rise in credit action may still spark an inflation impulse in few months time, analysts said.
On Thursday, the National Bank of Poland (NBP) said money supply grew 1.7 percent in August after a 2.3 percent rise in July and was 16.7 percent higher than at the end of last year.

"The 1.7 percent rise is within the norm...it shows the NBP and the finance ministry are co-operating to curb growth of money supply and inflation," Adam Berent, head of the analysis department at BIG Bank SA, told Reuters.
Analysts expected consumer prices to grow 0.6 percent in August after July's 0.1 percent fall. The Central Statistical Office is due to relase August inflation data on September 16.
They said however, that August's 4.0 percent rise in credit for the economy, including a 5.6 percent rise in credit for households, could speed up price growth in the fourth quarter.

"The rise in credit, especially consumption credit for households coupled with high real wage growth creates a good environment for a inflation impulse," said Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst of the Planning Ministry.
He said credit for households rose 64 percent in real terms from August 1995 and credit for enterprises by 15 percent.
The average wage in the enterprise sector was about 10 percent above year-on-year inflation in July.
"The July 16 (NBP) interest rate cut boosted inflationary growth of credit, but food price rises remain the main engine of inflation in the months to come," said Wojciech Babik, analyst at PBI SA.

Food prices have remained capped and rose only 0.1 percent from July 20-30 period to August 20-30, raising speculation that if money growth and inflation remained low in September, the NBP may have room to cut interest rates in October.
"September figres are likely to be pivotal, they may indicate whether the NBP would have room to manouever with interst rates," Chroscicki said.

In September 1995 prices jumped by three percent, meaning that a two percent rise this month could dip year-on-year inflation to around 19 percent from July's 20.4 percent and 21.6 percent in December 1995.
"If year-on-year CPI falls below 20 percent for good in September could lead to an interest rate cut as early as October," PBI's Babic said.
